passages.text: Associations Between <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Ser326Cys Polymorphism and Increased Body Mass Index and Fasting Glucose Level in the Japanese General Population
Background

Evidence suggests that Ser326Cys, a genetic polymorphism of human 8-oxoguanine glycosylase 1 (<italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic>), is associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes; however, the underlying mechanism is unclear. <sentence_start/>Recently, an animal study showed a significant association between the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype and obesity, although evidence for such an association in humans is limited. <sentence_start/>The purpose of this study was to examine the association between the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype and body mass index (BMI) and fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels.
Methods

Cross-sectional analysis was conducted using the baseline survey data from a Japan Multi-Institutional Collaborative Cohort Study, which included 1793 participants aged 40-69 years. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism was detected using a multiplex polymerase chain reaction-based invader assay. <sentence_start/>Multiple linear regression, analysis of covariance, and logistic regression were used to control for confounding variables.
Results

The Cys allele was significantly associated with increased BMI, FBG level, and total cholesterol (TC) level, even after adjustment for gender, age, energy intake, alcohol, smoking, physical activity, and family history of diabetes. <sentence_start/>An association with BMI was still observed after further adjustment for FBG and TC, but not for the study area (Amami or the mainland). <sentence_start/>The Cys/Cys genotype was significantly more prevalent in the participants with higher BMI (>27.5 kg/m<sup>2</sup>). <sentence_start/>However, the impact of genotype decreased and significance disappeared after adjusting for the study area.
Conclusions
The present results suggest that the study area being inside Japan confounds the association between <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype and obesity.
INTRODUCTION

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are known to play an essential role in the pathogenesis of diabetes.<citation rid="r01" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biocel.2006.07.001" pmid="16978905" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Several studies have reported that oxidative stress associated with insulin resistance, β cell dysfunction, impaired glucose tolerance, and mitochondrial dysfunction can ultimately lead to the diabetes disease state.<citation rid="r02" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2337/diabetes.52.1.1" pmid="12502486" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation><sup>-</sup><citation rid="r04" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.freeradbiomed.2010.12.006" pmid="21163346" pmcid="PMC3557825" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> ROS also cause strand breaks and base modifications in DNA, including the oxidation of guanine residues to 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanine (8-OHdG). <sentence_start/>These ROS-induced mutations alter the function of various genes and influence the pathogenesis of several diseases, such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative diseases, and diabetes.<citation rid="r01" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biocel.2006.07.001" pmid="16978905" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Base-excision repair (BER) plays an important role in preventing such disease, and human 8-oxoguanine glycosylase 1 (<italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic>) is one of the key glycosylases involved in the BER system.<citation rid="r05" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature05978" pmid="17581577" pmcid="PMC2896554" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The Ser326Cys polymorphism of the highly polymorphic OGG1 gene has been studied the most because this polymorphism is associated with functional differences in enzyme activity<citation rid="r06" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-04-0295" pmid="15734978" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation> and loss of function.<citation rid="r07" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/sj.onc.1201872" pmid="9681819" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, most epidemiological studies of this polymorphism have focused on cancer susceptibility.<citation rid="r08" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mc.20067" pmid="15584022" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation><sup>-</sup><citation rid="r12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035970" pmid="22540013" pmcid="PMC3335067" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation>

In the past decade, several studies have reported that the Ser326Cys <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism is associated with insulin resistance<citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10038-005-0335-8" pmid="16333523" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> and type 2 diabetes<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>-</sup><citation rid="r17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gene.2012.05.025" pmid="22652274" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation>; however, the underlying mechanism has not been elucidated. <sentence_start/>Obesity-associated insulin resistance is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes,<citation rid="r18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gad.1550907" pmid="17575046" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> and fat accumulation has been reported to be associated with systemic oxidative stress<citation rid="r19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.ATV.0000058402.34138.11" pmid="12615693" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI21625" pmid="15599400" pmcid="PMC535065" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation>; therefore, it may be possible to assess the risk of diabetes based on the association between the Ser326Cys <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism and body mass index (BMI). <sentence_start/>Recently, an animal study found that <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> deficiency alters cellular substrate metabolism, which favors a sparing phenotype and increased susceptibility to obesity<citation rid="r21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0051697" pmid="23284747" pmcid="PMC3524114" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation>; however, evidence for such association between <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism and BMI in humans is limited.<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation>

The purpose of this study was to determine whether the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Cys allele is associated with BMI and fasting glucose level. <sentence_start/>We also studied whether this association is modified by the effects of other factors.
METHODS
Study participants

The purpose of the Japan Multi-Institutional Collaborative Cohort (J-MICC) Study is to confirm and detect gene-environment interactions for lifestyle-related diseases using a large genome cohort, as previously described.<citation rid="r22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17696755" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Briefly, the J-MICC Study, which was initiated in 2005, included volunteers aged 35-69 years from 10 areas of Japan: Chiba, Shizuoka, Okazaki, Aichi, Takashima and Kyoto, which are located in Honshu Island; Tokushima, which is located in Shikoku Island; Fukuoka and Saga, which are located in Kyushu Island; and Amami, which is located 380 km southwest of Kyushu Island. <sentence_start/>Throughout this paper, we refer to Honshu Island, Shikoku Island, and Kyushu Island as “the mainland”. <sentence_start/>In this cross-sectional study, data from 4512 participants throughout these areas were collected during the period of 2005-2008.<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20100139" pmid="21467728" pmcid="PMC3899413" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. <sentence_start/>The study protocol was approved by the Nagoya University School of Medicine ethics committees and other participating institutions.
Questionnaire and measurements

A self-administered questionnaire was used to collect data on alcohol consumption, smoking, dietary habits, physical activity, current medication, disease history, and first-degree family history of diabetes. <sentence_start/>Details of the dietary assessment and estimation of physical activity were reported elsewhere.<citation rid="r24" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15075003" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation><sup>-</sup><citation rid="r27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20120078" pmid="23006958" pmcid="PMC3798564" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation>

Height and weight were measured to the nearest 0.1 cm and 0.1 kg, respectively. <sentence_start/>Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters (kg/m<sup>2</sup>). <sentence_start/>We defined a BMI of >27.5 kg/m<sup>2</sup> as obese; increased mortality has been reported above this point among East Asians.<citation rid="r28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1010679" pmid="21345101" pmcid="PMC4008249" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The HbA1c (%) and fasting blood glucose (FBG), triglyceride, total cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol levels were measured in laboratories in each study area, and the results of these measurements were collected. <sentence_start/>The HbA1c (%) value was converted from the Japan Diabetes Society (JDS) to the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) by using the following equation published by the JDS: NGSP (%) = 1.02 × JDS (%) + 0.25%.<citation rid="r29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.2040-1124.2012.00207.x" pmcid="PMC4014931" pmid="24843544" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation>
Genotyping

Genotyping was performed as described previously.<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20100139" pmid="21467728" pmcid="PMC3899413" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Single nucleotide polymorphisms, including the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Ser326Cys (rs1052133), were genotyped using a multiplex polymerase chain reaction-based Invader assay (Third Wave Technologies, Madison, WI, USA)<citation rid="r30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s100380170047" pmid="11501945" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation> at the Laboratory for Genotyping Development, Center for Genomic Medicine, RIKEN.
Statistical analysis

In the analysis, we excluded 2719 participants based on any of the following conditions: missing data of <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 11); missing FBG (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2627) data; taking type 2 diabetes medication (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 89); or a dietary energy intake greater than 4000 kcal/day (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2). <sentence_start/>Consequently, data for 976 men and 817 women aged 35-69 years were retained for analysis. <sentence_start/>Among these participants, data on alcohol consumption (17 men and 23 women) or physical activity (5 men and 5 women) were missing for some participants.

All analyses were performed with the SAS statistical software package (Ver. <sentence_start/>9.3 for Windows; SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). <sentence_start/>A <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

To compare the characteristics of participants according to the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype, we used the Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables and χ<sup>2</sup> tests for categorical variables. <sentence_start/>Adjusted means and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of BMI, FBG, and total cholesterol according to <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype were evaluated by least-squares general linear regression, and linear trends were assessed by the statistical significance of the regression coefficient of an ordinal variable for the factor under the following considerations: gender; age (continuous); energy intake (continuous); physical activity level (continuous); alcohol consumption status (never, former, or current drinker consuming 0.1-22.9, 23.0-45.9, or ≥46.0 g ethanol/day); smoking status (never, former, or current smoker of 1-19, 20-39, or ≥40 cigarettes/day); first-degree family history of diabetes (positive, negative, or unknown); study area (Amami or the mainland); BMI (continuous, for the evaluation of FBG and total cholesterol); FBG (continuous, for BMI and total cholesterol); and total cholesterol (continuous, for BMI and FBG). <sentence_start/>Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs of <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype for excessive BMI (>27.5 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) were estimated using logistic regression models adjusted for potential confounders (age, BMI, energy intake, alcohol consumption, smoking, physical activity, family history of diabetes, and study area).
RESULTS

The characteristics of study participants according to the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Ser326Cys genotype are shown in Table 1. <sentence_start/>The genotype distributions of the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Ser326Cys gene among all participants followed the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (χ<sup>2</sup> = 0.511, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.475). <sentence_start/>Genotype frequency was significantly different in the Amami area (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>The Cys allele carriers had significantly higher mean BMI (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.021) and FBG (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.001) levels, and a higher proportion were current alcohol drinkers (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>TC level tended to be higher in Cys allele carriers, although this difference was not statistically significant (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.077).

After adjusting for possible confounding factors, such as gender, age, energy intake, physical activity level, ethanol intake, smoking, and family history of diabetes, the Cys allele was found to be significantly associated with higher BMI, FBG, and TC levels in a dose-dependent manner (all <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.05, Table 2, Model 2). <sentence_start/>The association with BMI was still significant after further adjustment for FBG and TC (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.02, Model 3). <sentence_start/>However, the significance disappeared after adjusting for study area (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.23, Model 4).

Data for the evaluation of the association between obesity (BMI > 27.5 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype using logistic regression analysis are shown in Table 3. <sentence_start/>The prevalence of obesity in the Cys/Cys genotype was significantly greater after adjusting for gender, age, energy intake, physical activity level, ethanol intake, smoking, family history of diabetes, FBG, and TC (Model 3). <sentence_start/>Although Cys allele carriers tended to have a higher proportion of obesity, the significance of this association disappeared after adjusting for the study area (Model 4). <sentence_start/>The OR of the Amami area for obesity was 2.44 (95% CI 1.67-3.56), which was greater than that of the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype.
DISCUSSION

In this cross-sectional study, we observed significant associations between the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Cys/Cys genotype and higher BMI and incidence of obesity, after adjustment for possible confounding factors other than the study area. <sentence_start/>After adjusting for study area, however, this significance disappeared, suggesting that study area is a confounding factor. <sentence_start/>Despite this lack of association, Cys allele carriers tended to have a higher proportion of obesity than Ser/Ser.

Several epidemiological studies have examined the associations between the Ser326Cys <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism and insulin resistance<citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10038-005-0335-8" pmid="16333523" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> and type 2 diabetes.<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>-</sup><citation rid="r17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gene.2012.05.025" pmid="22652274" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> Wang et al reported that the Cys/Cys variant significantly decreases insulin sensitivity, even after adjustment for possible confounders, including BMI, among the Taiwanese.<citation rid="r13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10038-005-0335-8" pmid="16333523" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Three studies detected significant association between Ser326Cys <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> polymorphism and diabetes.<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000291964" pmid="20606456" pmcid="PMC3083264" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gene.2012.05.025" pmid="22652274" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Specifically, Daimon et al reported that decreased insulin secretion is associated with being a Cys allele carrier, measured by homeostatic model assessment beta cell function (HOMA-β) in a Japanese population,<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> while Gönül et al reported a significant association between the Cys allele and insulin resistance in a Turkish population, measured by HOMA-R.<citation rid="r17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gene.2012.05.025" pmid="22652274" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>On the other hand, one case-control study conducted in a Polish population failed to detect an association between this polymorphism and diabetes<citation rid="r15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19514640" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> due to limited sample size. <sentence_start/>Regarding obesity, an animal study showed significant association between the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype and obesity,<citation rid="r21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0051697" pmid="23284747" pmcid="PMC3524114" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> and one epidemiological study reported a positive association between BMI and this polymorphism.<citation rid="r14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.05.119" pmid="19486888" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Our study showed no evidence of an association between this polymorphism and increased BMI and FBG.

In the present study, the study area had a significant impact on the prevalence of obesity. <sentence_start/>Among the studies reporting genetic differences between the Amami and the mainland populations,<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20100139" pmid="21467728" pmcid="PMC3899413" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1271/bbb.70550" pmid="18256468" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035000" pmid="22509376" pmcid="PMC3318002" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation> two used data from the J-MICC study.<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20100139" pmid="21467728" pmcid="PMC3899413" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="r32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035000" pmid="22509376" pmcid="PMC3318002" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Nishiyama et al found a low but significant level of genetic differentiation between the mainland population and the population of the Amami Islands,<citation rid="r32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035000" pmid="22509376" pmcid="PMC3318002" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation> while Wakai et al reported that some polymorphisms showed a substantial difference in minor allele frequency among the participating cohorts.<citation rid="r23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2188/jea.JE20100139" pmid="21467728" pmcid="PMC3899413" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>They proposed that genetic variation among the study areas should be considered when analyzing the data from the J-MICC study. <sentence_start/>According to the Japanese Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (JSNP) database, the frequency of <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotypes of Ser/Ser, Ser/Cys, and Cys/Cys was reported for 18%, 59%, and 23% of participants, respectively.<citation rid="r33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/30.1.158" pmid="11752280" pmcid="PMC99126" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In this study, the genotype frequency of Ser/Ser, Ser/Cys, and Cys/Cys polymorphisms in mainland Japan was 22.7%, 50.7%, and 26.6%, while those on Amami Island were 13.4%, 41.2%, and 45.4%, respectively. <sentence_start/>We found that the variation in the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype Cys/Cys frequency between the Amami and the mainland could lead to a false-positive result if the study area was not considered. <sentence_start/>This is known as confounding by population stratification,<citation rid="r34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(03)12520-2" pmid="12598158" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation> which needs to be carefully considered in genetic epidemiology, even in the relatively homogeneous Japanese population. <sentence_start/>A significantly higher BMI in the Amami area may reflect population differences in genetic or environmental factors; therefore, further investigation is needed.

This study has several methodological limitations. <sentence_start/>First, the cross-sectional nature of our study limits our ability to determine causation, even though we excluded participants who were on medication for type 2 diabetes. <sentence_start/>In addition, we did not have appropriate replication data accompanying this study. <sentence_start/>Second, although measuring fat accumulation using computed tomography scans or echograms is ideal, we used BMI to evaluate obesity. <sentence_start/>Misclassification of obesity may have therefore occurred; however, misclassification of obesity would be expected to lower estimations for the association. <sentence_start/>Third, there may be intrinsic information bias in our assessments of lifestyle-related factors, such as dietary and family history. <sentence_start/>However, if any misclassification were present, it would be non-differential by the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> genotype and would likely underestimate the true associations. <sentence_start/>Finally, although we adjusted for potential confounding factors in the multivariate analysis, residual confounding factors by known or unknown risk factors may have been present.

In conclusion, these results suggest that the <italic toggle="yes">hOGG1</italic> Ser/Cys genotype may have some influence on obesity, although its contribution is smaller than the influence of the study area. <sentence_start/>While our study found no associations of this genotype with BMI or FBG levels, we did find evidence of confounding by population stratification for these associations. <sentence_start/>This report may provide important information for genetic association analysis in the Japanese population.
